content.title: KALM’s technical contributions. (1/4)
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed and thoughtful review of our submission, *KALM: Knowledge-Aware Integration of Local, Document, and Global Contexts for Long Document Understanding*. We address the raised questions and concerns below.

```
The novelty of combining three types of knowledge is limited. Introducing entity description, sub-graph and document-level graph are all leveraged in the previous papers, and the combination techniques are also not new.
```

We would like to clarify that the novelty of the KALM model is not limited to a combination of three existing components. KALM makes three key conceptual contributions:

First, KALM introduced the novel **knowledge coreference** framework for document-level analysis. Different paragraphs may discuss the same or overlapping entities and concepts, which represent the logic flow underpinning long documents. KALM enables this analysis through knowledge coreference document graphs (Section 2.2) and a graph neural network architecture with knowledge-guided message passing (Section 2.3.1), compared to existing works that treat long documents as a sequential list of paragraphs without deeper relationships or interactions [1,2].

Second, motivated by the fact that different document contexts may play different roles and have varying importance in different tasks, we propose the novel **ContextFusion layer** to enable interpretable and interactive information exchange across contexts. Compared to prior work which simply uses concatenation or linear layers [2,3], the ContextFusion layer incorporates better interaction between contexts of varying granularity, helping improve model performance (Table 2) and shedding light on the roles and importance of each context (Figure 2).

Finally, we indeed combined three document contexts, and the combination of three levels of document contexts is novel. Table 8 provided a checklist of baseline methods and the document contexts that they leverage. To the best of our knowledge, KALM is the first work to jointly consider local, document, and global contexts, the importance of which is substantiated by the performance gains in extensive experiments.

We have streamlined the method description in Section 2 to better highlight KALM’s unique technical contributions in our revised paper.

[1] Wenqian Zhang et al. 2022. KCD: Knowledge Walks and Textual Cues Enhanced Political Perspective Detection in News Media. In Proceedings of the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, pages 4129–4140, Seattle, United States. Association for Computational Linguistics.

[2] Hu, Linmei, et al. “Compare to the knowledge: Graph neural fake news detection with external knowledge.” Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2021.

[3] Zhang, X., et al. “GreaseLM: Graph REASoning Enhanced Language Models for Question Answering.” International Conference on Representation Learning (ICLR). 2022.

content.comment:
```
Unclear how the incorporation of external domain aligns with document domains? For example: to introduce entity and subgraph representation for entity 'apple'? How dies it tackle domain relatedness of raw data and external knowledge to control drift?
```

In this work, we assume access to an external KB that is highly relevant to the domain of the document understanding tasks (Section 2.1). In practice, we used the same KBs adopted in state-of-the-art task-specific baselines on the three tasks [1,2,3], which are KGAP [4], CompareNet [2], and ConceptNet [5]. We agree that there might be domain shifts between tasks and KBs: there are so many NLP datasets and so many KBs, while which KB(s) would be helpful or in-domain for a given NLP task/dataset remains unclear upfront and a suitable KB is often manually selected. For future research, we are planning on automatically discovering which KBs are highly relevant and helpful to a given task/dataset and which knowledge injection approach is most appropriate for different scenarios, which is not within the scope of this work.

content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed and thoughtful review of our submission, *KALM: Knowledge-Aware Integration of Local, Document, and Global Contexts for Long Document Understanding*. We address the raised questions and concerns below.

```
The paper is mostly clear. But I find some parts may be improved. For example, the categorization of local context, document-level context, and global context is kind of confusing. To my understanding, local context and global context leverages external knowledge, the former focuses on mentioned entities and the latter also includes related entities that are not explicitly mentioned. Document-level context does not use external knowledge but use the internal relations between sentences. In other words, local & global=>external, document-level => internal.
```

You are 100% right and spot-on regarding the local and global context.

It is true that document-level context “use(s) the internal relations between sentences”, but these “relations between entities” are grounded in external KBs. For example, “Johannes Kepler” is an entity in the Wikidata KB, and if both paragraphs i and j mention “Johannes Kepler”, they are connected with the edge type “Johannes Kepler”. An alternative to this would be using named entity recognition and coreference resolution to identify all entities regardless of whether they are in KBs or not. We tested this setting, which resulted in too much noise in the document-level context input, which is similarly observed by [1]. In addition, restricting it to only entities in the KB also allows for the knowledge-guided message-passing mechanism in Section 2.3.1, which is one of KALM’s unique technical contributions.

We improved Section 2.2 to better clarify this about the document-level context.

content.title: KALM is more than a new and unified approach. (2/3)
content.comment:
```
The novelty is limited given all three kinds of information has been considered in previous work. but this paper proposes a new and unified approach.
```

We absolutely agree that KALM is “a new and unified approach” towards knowledge-aware long document understanding with various shades of document contexts. In addition, KALM makes three key conceptual contributions:

First, KALM introduced the novel **knowledge coreference** framework for document-level analysis. Different paragraphs may discuss the same or overlapping entities and concepts, which represent the logic flow underpinning long documents. KALM enables this analysis through knowledge coreference document graphs (Section 2.2) and a graph neural network architecture with knowledge-guided message passing (Section 2.3.1), compared to existing works that treat long documents as a sequential list of paragraphs without deeper relationships or interactions [1,2].

Second, motivated by the fact that different document contexts may play different roles and have varying importance in different tasks, we propose the novel **ContextFusion layer** to enable interpretable and interactive information exchange across contexts. Compared to prior work which simply uses concatenation or linear layers [2,3], the ContextFusion layer incorporates better interaction between contexts of varying granularity, helping improve model performance (Table 2) and shedding light on the roles and importance of each context (Figure 2).

Finally, we indeed combined three document contexts, and the combination of three levels of document contexts is novel. Table 8 provided a checklist of baseline methods and the document contexts that they leverage. To the best of our knowledge, KALM is the first work to jointly consider local, document, and global contexts, the importance of which is substantiated by the performance gains in extensive experiments.

We have streamlined the method description in Section 2 to better highlight KALM’s unique technical contributions in our revised paper.

content.title: Rationale behind merging 2-hop KB subgraphs. (1/5)
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed and thoughtful review of our submission, *KALM: Knowledge-Aware Integration of Local, Document, and Global Contexts for Long Document Understanding*. We address the raised questions and concerns below.

```
This paper has mentioned some resolutions, but didn’t introduce the reasons, for example, KALM merges their 2-hop neighborhood to obtain a KG subgraph, why is 2-hop? Just tricks?
```

KALM supports k-hop knowledge graph subgraphs with all values of k. In practice, we used k=2 for the following reasons:

If k=0 [1,2], only the directly mentioned entity is considered, which breaks the structure of KGs and could not introduce unmentioned yet connecting entities to document understanding.

If k>2, due to the exponential neighborhood expansion process, the number of entities eventually included in the KG subgraph would be too large, introducing a lot of irrelevant information to the global context. In addition, applying a k-layer GNN on k-hop KB subgraphs with too large k would result in over-smoothing [3,4] and lower representation learning performance.

As a result, k=1 or 2 would be ideal. Since k=2 includes relatively more entities and connections, we adopted k=2 which is also the norm in previous works [5,6]. We explained the reasoning behind k=2 in Section 2.2 of the revised paper.

To answer the reviewer’s questions about why different contexts might have different roles/importance in different tasks: we hypothesize that the importance and relevance of each type of context varies, depending on the nature of the task.

For political perspective detection, LMs are required to identify political leaning in news articles. Since news media often try to appear impartial on the surface [1] while occasionally giving away their subtle bias in certain sentences, political perspective detection might focus more on the local context and sentence-by-sentence analysis.

For misinformation detection, fake news often contains elements or claims that are not consistent with the rest of the article due to manipulations by malicious actors [2]. As a result, it should focus more on the document-level context to identify the subtle inconsistencies between the lines in the whole document.

For roll call vote prediction, legislation texts often involve a lot of concepts and jargon that rarely appear in LM pretraining data [3]. As a result, it should focus more on the global context and connect issues discussed in the legislation documents to external KBs to better understand the relations between these issues.

Given that different contexts might have different importance/role in different tasks/datasets, we conducted experiments in Figure 2, which supports this hypothesis and reveals that different document contexts do have unique patterns on different tasks/datasets, further strengthening the argument for jointly considering the three contexts.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this study the authors investigate an approach to model different levels of granularity of interactions in documents with the goal to improve document level classification tasks. They achieve this with an architecture that models the text in a document with three levels of granularity: paragraph level, document level and global level. In the paragraph level, the tokens are encoded with a Transformer and pooled into one embedding. In the document level, a document graph is built using the paragraph embeddings as the node representations and edges between them exists if both paragraphs mention the same entity. The global level extracts a subgraph around the mentioned entities in the document and embeds them with a knowledge graph embedding model.  To also allow for interaction between those layers they allow for attention based aggregation to let information flow in either direction. The model is trained on training data for a respective task, and not pretrained in any way beforehand (other than the knowledge graph embeddings I suppose)
They show results on different kinds of document level benchmarks, in which their approach consistently outperforms other approaches (generic baselines based on pretrained LMs as well other approaches designed for such tasks). They also do an ablation to show the effectiveness of each of the levels of interaction, as well as an brief investigation into the attention patters across the different levels.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

S1. All those levels of knowledge interaction represent different modes of interaction between entities and also their context in the paragraph, document and knowledge graph, which is the interesting aspect of this study. 
S2. To allow for information flow between these different levels is also interesting, and seems to be working according to the ablation and the attention introspection. 
S3. According to their evaluation, the approach outperforms other approaches by a decent margin, which makes it seem as a very attractive approach.

Weaknesses:

W1. The proposed approach consists of so many moving parts that judging its soundness is very difficult. A comprehensive writeup that would adequately present each of the components and design choices with a dedicated discussion and experiments why other alternatives have been ruled out would likely go into the 30 page dimension. 

W2. Having worked with LM+KGs, long document representation (the latter non-published) I have to say to be surprised that their approach works so well. It is really difficult to even establish benchmarks that really require document level understanding, let alone to demonstrate the need for knowledge graph representation. Way to often information seemingly requiring document level understanding and knowledge graphs can be covered easily by common sense and general knowledge acquired by pretrained language models, as well as their ability to exploit lexical hints that we humans use to not require the understanding of a full document. The evaluation with Roberta, Deberta ect seem to rule that out, but then again, there is no information how these numbers have been obtained. Did those documents fit into the 512 tokens?
